detail: re-judged from diff.patch on a recovered board: 90 readings reported in order with correct temperatures (first judgement hit a wedged USB port)
finalText:
## Root cause

The queue stored `char *` pointers, and `sensor_task` always sent the address of its **single shared stack buffer** `line`:

```c
char line[48];
...
char *msg = line;
xQueueSend(readings, &msg, ...);   // copies the pointer, not the text
```

`xQueueSend` copies only the pointer value. Every queued item pointed at the same 48-byte stack buffer, which the next loop iteration immediately overwrote. By the time `report_task` woke up (it even sleeps 30 ms before printing), the buffer held the last reading written, so each burst printed the same `seq`/`temp` repeatedly (e.g. five copies of `seq=4`), and earlier readings were lost.

A secondary defect was `QUEUE_LEN 4` for a burst of 5, which forced the last send to rely on a 10 ms timeout and could drop a reading.

## What I changed (`main/main.c`)

- Replaced the pointer-based queue with a by-value `reading_t { uint32_t seq; int temp; }`. `xQueueSend` now copies the actual reading, so each queued entry stays intact.
- `report_task` receives a `reading_t` and formats the same `report seq=<n> temp=<t>` line, preserving the line format.
- Set `QUEUE_LEN` to `FIFO_BURST` (5) so a full burst fits without timeout drops.
- Burst size (5) and burst interval (500 ms) are unchanged.

## Verification on the board

Flashed and captured serial output: readings now appear exactly once, in order, each with its own temperature, e.g. `seq=0 temp=20.00`, `seq=1 temp=20.37`, `seq=2 temp=20.74`, … A 12-second capture yielded 123 consecutive seq values (132→254), all unique, strictly `+1`, with zero `dropped` warnings.
